materiality_analysis.reason: The disclosure reveals a strategic shift in deposit drivers across business segments. In 2024, CCB deposits declined due to spending; in 2025, CCB deposits increased driven by new accounts. Additionally, CIB drivers updated from structured note maturities to Securities Services inflows. These changes reflect significant shifts in client funding behavior and segment performance.
materiality_analysis.key_change: Shift in deposit drivers from CCB decline to growth and CIB composition change

comparisons.peer_summary: Deposits increased by $41.6 billion, primarily driven by growth in commercial client balances and time deposits.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPMorgan and Bank of America reported an overall increase in total deposits for 2024, but they differ significantly in the specific drivers cited. JPMorgan attributes its deposit growth to specific segment-level inflows in Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB) from Payments and structured notes, and growth in Asset & Wealth Management (AWM) from higher-yielding products, while noting a decline in Consumer & Community Banking (CCB) due to spending. In contrast, Bank of America attributes its $41.6 billion increase primarily to general 'commercial client balances and time deposits' without segment-level granularity in the provided text.

sentences.text: • an increase in CIB due to net inflows predominantly in Payments and net issuances of structured notes as a result of client demand in Markets, partially offset by deposit attrition, which included actions taken to reduce certain deposits,

• an increase in AWM as a result of growth in balances in new and existing client accounts, reflecting the impact of higher-yielding product offerings, largely offset by continued migration into other investments, and
• a decline in CCB primarily driven by a decrease in balances in existing accounts due to increased customer spending, largely offset by new accounts.
Deposits increased $41.6 billion primarily driven by growth in commercial client balances and time deposits.

comparisons.peer_summary: Average deposits were relatively flat year-over-year but increased 1% sequentially. In Q4 2024, Services deposits grew due to TTS and Securities Services gains, USPB declined due to transfers to Wealth, Wealth increased due to those transfers, and All Other decreased due to wind-downs, FX, and CD reductions.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPMorgan and Citigroup provide detailed segment-level breakdowns of deposit trends in 2024. JPMorgan reports a decline in CCB driven by increased customer spending, whereas Citigroup reports a decline in its US Personal Banking (USPB) segment driven by transfers of relationships and deposits to its Wealth segment. Both disclosures also identify 'migration' or shifts to other investment products as key offsetting factors; JPMorgan notes AWM growth was offset by migration to other investments, while Citigroup notes Wealth segment growth was offset by shifts to higher-yielding investments.

• USPB decreased 18% year-over-year, as the transfer of certain relationships and the associated deposits to Wealth more than offset underlying deposit growth.

• Wealth increased 3% year-over-year, largely reflecting the transfer of certain relationships and the associated deposits from USPB, partially offset by the shift in deposits to higher-yielding investments on Citi's platform.

comparisons.peer_summary: Time deposits are predominantly brokered certificates of deposit, while total deposits in 2024 increased due to higher Savings and Time deposits, offset by reductions in Brokerage sweep deposits driven by client outflows to alternative products.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley disclose that deposit growth in specific areas was offset by client outflows to alternative investment products. JPMorgan notes that AWM deposit growth was 'largely offset by continued migration into other investments,' while Morgan Stanley states that total deposit increases were 'partially offset by a reduction in Brokerage sweep deposits, largely due to net outflows to alternative cash equivalent and other investment products.' However, JPMorgan reports an overall increase in average and period-end deposits for 2024, whereas Morgan Stanley's disclosure focuses on the composition mix (Savings/Time up, Brokerage sweep down) rather than a clear net direction for the total.
